GEO and AEO are not a myth.
Neil Patel's 24 sitemaps prove it.

People say GEO and AEO are unclear, uncertain, and unproven. Neil Patel — one of the most followed digital marketing voices on the planet — has a dedicated stats page publishing verified GEO and AEO data from real campaigns. His site runs 24 sitemaps. Nine post sitemaps alone. The confusion is not because GEO is a myth. It is because most people implementing it have no idea what they are actually doing.

// The evidence nobody is reading

Neil Patel co-founded Crazy Egg, Hello Bar, and NP Digital — one of the largest digital marketing agencies in the world by client revenue. He has been writing about SEO and content marketing since 2006. His personal site receives millions of visitors monthly. When Neil Patel publishes data about what works in digital marketing, it is not speculation — it is aggregated from the campaigns NP Digital runs for real clients across hundreds of industries.

His marketing stats section includes a dedicated page titled "does structured data help with GEO." Another titled "GEO AEO driven leads growth." Another titled "content metrics GEO vs SEO." Another titled "GEO traffic vs conversion rates." Another titled "how marketers are increasing their GEO traffic." These are not theoretical pages. Each one publishes a specific data point from a specific study — the kind of data that gets produced when you run GEO campaigns for real businesses and measure the results.

The people who say GEO is uncertain are not reading Neil Patel's stats pages. They are not implementing GEO correctly. They are confusing "I tried adding schema and nothing happened" with "GEO does not work." Those are not the same statement.

Neil Patel's sitemap stack — the other lesson in plain sight

// Chapter 01 — 24 sitemaps, one domain

Before getting into the GEO data itself, the sitemap structure is worth examining because it demonstrates the same authority network principle covered in the previous article on King Kong's strategy — but taken to a different dimension.

King Kong built wide — hundreds of geographic location pages, systematic city-level coverage. Neil Patel built deep — nine post sitemaps (each maxed out with URLs), plus dedicated sitemaps for every course series, every stats category, every content type. The result is the same: a domain with so many indexed pages targeting so many specific queries that something on neilpatel.com appears for an enormous percentage of digital marketing searches.

The man who knows the most about digital marketing has not stopped building pages for fifteen years. The people who say GEO is uncertain stopped after publishing three blog posts.

Why the confusion exists — the implementation gap

// Chapter 03 — What people are actually doing wrong

GEO and AEO are not new ideas. Google's Featured Snippets — which are AEO by another name — have existed since 2014. The practice of structuring content to answer specific questions directly, with the right schema markup, has been a documented ranking factor for years. What changed in 2023 and 2024 was the addition of AI models as citation sources — ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Google AI Overviews — which expanded the surface area where your content either gets cited or does not.

The confusion comes from people who tried adding schema markup to one page and saw no immediate change in AI citations, concluded that GEO does not work, and moved on. That is like someone putting one brick in the ground and concluding that houses do not exist. GEO is a compounding infrastructure investment. The businesses that are winning in AI search right now started building consistent structured data six months or a year ago and never stopped.

// Why GEO "doesn't work" for most people
The implementation failure list
  • Added schema to homepage only, not every page
  • Schema keywords do not match page content keywords
  • No entity disambiguation — Google cannot tell who you are
  • No Wikidata entity — no machine-readable anchor
  • No llms.txt — AI crawlers do not know what to index
  • No FAQPage schema — missing the AEO entry point
  • Published three pages and stopped
  • Measured after two weeks, concluded it failed
// Why GEO works when implemented correctly
The implementation success list
  • Schema on every single page, schema keywords match content
  • Entity disambiguation — distinct Wikidata entity registered
  • llms.txt tells AI crawlers exactly what the site covers
  • FAQPage schema on every article targeting real search queries
  • LocalBusiness or Service schema with full geo-coordinates
  • Internal links connecting related pages across the domain
  • Consistent publishing — measured in months not days
  • GSC submitted on every new page within 24 hours of publishing

GEO, AEO, and SEO — what each one actually means

// Chapter 04 — Plain English definitions that stop the confusion

Part of the confusion is genuine terminological overlap. SEO, AEO, and GEO describe overlapping practices with different primary targets. Here is the plain English version:

SEO Traditional
Search Engine Optimisation — ranking in Google's blue links
The practice of building pages that rank in traditional Google search results — the ten blue links. Involves keyword research, backlinks, page speed, mobile optimisation, and content quality. Still essential. Still works. Neil Patel's nine post sitemaps are largely built for SEO traffic. This is where the authority network strategy from the King Kong article lives.
AEO Answers
Answer Engine Optimisation — appearing in answer boxes
The practice of structuring content to appear directly in Google's Featured Snippets, People Also Ask boxes, and AI Overviews. Requires content structured as a direct answer to a specific question — not just content that mentions the keyword. FAQPage schema is the primary technical implementation. When someone asks Google "does structured data help with GEO" and Google returns a box with a direct answer — that is AEO working.
GEO AI Models
Generative Engine Optimisation — getting cited by AI
The practice of structuring your site so that AI models — ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Grok — can find, understand, and cite your business when users ask relevant questions. Requires entity disambiguation (Wikidata), structured schema across all pages, llms.txt, robots.txt configured for AI crawlers, and content that AI models can extract specific answers from. When someone asks ChatGPT "who builds websites in Cape Town" and your business appears — that is GEO working.

The South African GEO opportunity right now

// Chapter 05 — The window that is closing

Neil Patel's stats page on GEO adoption by company size shows something important: smaller companies are significantly behind larger ones in GEO implementation. The businesses that are being cited by AI models today started building the infrastructure before most of their competitors understood what GEO was.

In South Africa, that gap is even wider. The SA digital marketing conversation is still largely about Facebook ads, Instagram reels, and whether to use WordPress or Wix. Almost nobody is talking about structured data schema, Wikidata entity registration, or llms.txt files. That is the opportunity — and it is closing as GEO adoption grows globally.

The businesses that build the GEO infrastructure now will dominate AI-referred traffic for their category in South Africa for years. Not because the strategy is secret — Neil Patel publishes the data publicly. Because the strategy requires consistent, technically correct implementation over months, and most businesses will not do it. The same dynamic that makes authority networks effective in traditional SEO makes GEO effective in AI search. The gap between the businesses doing it and the businesses not doing it is where the opportunity lives.
